name: Tools: plan and design
description: Roadmaps, research, docs, wikis, diagrams, prototyping.

cards.subject: A product roadmap
says: communicates the direction and priorities of a product over time
is a plan that is expected to change as the team learns
is read mostly by stakeholders who do not edit it
cards.use: need to show stakeholders where the product is heading
not: is a binding contract of delivery dates

cards.subject: A backlog
says: holds the ordered list of work not yet done
is reordered as priorities change
is detailed at the top and rough at the bottom
cards.use: need one ordered list of what to build after the current work
not: must be fully specified before any item can be started

cards.subject: A now-next-later roadmap
says: groups work by how soon it will be tackled rather than by calendar date
avoids promising dates for items further away
has three columns that signal certainty falling with distance
cards.use: want to show direction without committing to dates
not: attaches an exact release date to every card

cards.subject: MoSCoW prioritisation
says: sorts requirements into must, should, could and will-not-have-this-time
makes explicit what is out of scope for now
cards.use: need to agree the minimum set of requirements for a release
not: gives every requirement a numeric score

cards.subject: An impact-effort matrix
says: plots ideas on a grid of expected value against cost to deliver
highlights quick wins in the high-value, low-effort corner
cards.use: want a fast visual way to compare ideas in a workshop
not: calculates a score from reach and confidence

cards.subject: RICE scoring
says: scores an idea on reach, impact, confidence and effort
divides the estimated benefit by the effort
discounts ideas whose benefit is a guess by using a confidence factor
cards.use: need to compare many ideas with a repeatable formula
not: sorts items into must-have and nice-to-have buckets

cards.subject: An outcome-based roadmap
says: lists the problems to solve or results to achieve rather than the features to ship
leaves the solution open for the team to discover
cards.use: want the team to own a problem instead of a fixed feature list
not: is just a feature list with a different title

cards.subject: The Kano model
says: classifies features as basic expectations, performance features or delighters
predicts that a delighter tends to become an expectation over time
cards.use: need to judge which features customers merely expect and which would delight them
not: scores features by reach and effort

cards.subject: An opportunity solution tree
says: maps a desired outcome to customer opportunities, then to solutions and experiments
keeps the link between evidence and the idea being tested visible
cards.use: want to show how an idea traces back to a customer need
not: lists releases in date order

cards.subject: A user interview
says: asks one person open questions about their behaviour and context
yields rich qualitative detail from a small number of people
cards.use: need to learn why people do something
not: measures how common a behaviour is across the whole user base

cards.subject: A survey
says: collects answers to fixed questions from many people
gives numbers but little explanation of why
cards.use: need to measure how common an opinion or behaviour is
not: reveals the unspoken reasons behind a behaviour

cards.subject: A persona
says: summarises a segment of users as a representative profile
is only as trustworthy as the research it is built from
cards.use: want the team to keep a specific kind of user in mind while designing
not: is a real customer whose details are shared with the whole team

cards.subject: Usability testing
says: watches people attempt realistic tasks with a design
reveals where users get stuck or confused
cards.use: need to know whether people can complete a task
not: measures how many people would buy the product

cards.subject: A card sort
says: asks people to group topics into categories that feel natural to them
informs the labels and grouping of navigation
cards.use: need to decide how to group and name navigation items
not: checks whether people can find an item in a finished hierarchy

cards.subject: A tree test
says: checks whether people can find items in a proposed hierarchy without any visual design
measures how findable content is under a given structure
cards.use: need to validate a navigation structure before designing screens
not: asks people to invent their own categories

cards.subject: An A/B test
says: compares two variants by showing them to separate random groups of users
needs enough traffic to reach a reliable conclusion
cards.use: want quantitative evidence about which variant performs better
not: explains why users prefer one variant

cards.subject: A diary study
says: has participants record their own experiences over days or weeks
captures behaviour that cannot be observed in one session
cards.use: need to understand behaviour that unfolds over a long period
not: observes the participant in the room as they work

cards.subject: Contextual inquiry
says: observes people doing their real work in their own setting
uncovers workarounds that people forget to mention in an interview
cards.use: need to see how a task is really done rather than how people describe it
not: asks participants to complete a fixed script of tasks in a lab

cards.subject: A feedback inbox
says: gathers requests from many channels into one place
stops feedback from being lost in individual email threads
cards.use: want everyone's customer comments to land in one list
not: decides which requests will be built
like: Interview notes and feedback in Moksy

cards.subject: Feedback tagging
says: lets you count how often a theme appears
works best with a small agreed vocabulary of tags
cards.use: need to see which problems come up most often
not: replaces reading the original comments

cards.subject: A support ticket as feedback
says: records a problem in the customer's own words
over-represents people who ran into trouble
cards.use: want evidence of what is going wrong for customers today
not: represents the opinions of customers who are satisfied and silent

cards.subject: A voting board
says: lets users upvote requests made by others
shows how many people want something but not why
cards.use: want a rough public signal of demand for requests
not: explains the underlying need behind each request

cards.subject: Closing the loop
says: tells people who gave feedback what was decided and why
encourages them to keep sharing feedback
cards.use: want contributors to see their input led somewhere
not: is only needed for requests that get built

cards.subject: Anonymising participants
says: removes names and identifying details from research notes
lets findings be shared more widely with less privacy risk
cards.use: need to share interview notes beyond the research team
not: makes it unnecessary to ask for consent

cards.subject: Separating a request from the need
says: asks what the customer is trying to achieve behind the solution they suggested
opens up options better than the one proposed
cards.use: hear a customer ask for a specific feature
not: means ignoring suggestions customers make

cards.subject: Recording retention
says: limits how long raw recordings are kept
supports deleting a participant's data on request
cards.use: need a rule for how long to keep interview recordings
not: applies only to published reports

cards.subject: A README
says: explains what a project is and how to start using it
sits at the top of a repository where newcomers look first
cards.use: want a newcomer to get started without asking anyone
not: is the full design history of the project
like: The gglearn docs folder and README

cards.subject: A wiki
says: is a set of linked pages that many people can edit
suits material that changes often and is written by non-developers
cards.use: need a shared place for meeting notes, onboarding and plans
not: is the best home for text that must stay true alongside code

cards.subject: A decision log
says: records what was decided, when and why
saves the team from reopening settled questions
cards.use: want a running list of the choices a team has made
not: describes the steps to handle an incident

cards.subject: A page owner
says: is one named person responsible for a page staying correct
gives readers someone to ask about the content
cards.use: find that nobody updates a shared page
not: means only that person may ever edit the page

cards.subject: A last-reviewed date
says: tells the reader how fresh a page is
helps readers judge whether to trust the content
cards.use: want readers to judge if a page is still current
not: proves that the content is correct

cards.subject: Docs as code
says: keeps documentation in version control and reviews it with the code
lets one pull request change both a feature and its docs
cards.use: need documentation that must stay true alongside code
not: moves all documentation out of the repository into a wiki

cards.subject: An architecture decision record
says: captures one decision with its context, the options considered and the consequences
is kept as a short dated file in the repository
cards.use: want to preserve the reasoning behind a technical choice for future developers
not: is updated in place whenever the decision changes without keeping history

cards.subject: A runbook
says: lists the steps to handle a known operational task or incident
is written to be followed under pressure
cards.use: want an on-call person to handle a known failure without guessing
not: explains the product vision to new staff

cards.subject: The four kinds of documentation
says: separates tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation
gives each type of reader need its own kind of page
cards.use: find that one page tries to teach, instruct and describe at once
not: says every page should contain all four in equal parts

cards.subject: A meeting note
says: records decisions, owners and next steps rather than a transcript
is useful to people who did not attend
cards.use: want absent colleagues to catch up on what was agreed
not: is a word-for-word transcript of the discussion

cards.subject: An action item
says: names one owner and a due date for a task agreed in a meeting
is checked at the start of the next meeting
cards.use: agree a task in a meeting
not: is complete once it has been discussed

cards.subject: A folder
says: puts each note in exactly one place
expresses a single hierarchy of categories
cards.use: want a simple structure where every note has one home
not: lets one note appear under several categories at once

cards.subject: A tag
says: lets one note belong to several categories at once
can be searched across all folders
cards.use: want one note to be findable under more than one topic
not: moves the note to a different location

cards.subject: Backlinks
says: show every note that links to the one being read
reveal connections without a manual index
cards.use: want to see which notes refer to the page you are viewing
not: are links that point to external websites

cards.subject: A permanent note
says: states one idea in the writer's own words and links to related notes
grows a personal knowledge base over time
cards.use: want notes that remain useful long after the source is forgotten
not: copies a quotation from a source unchanged

cards.subject: A flowchart
says: shows steps and decisions in a process using arrows between shapes
uses a diamond for a yes-or-no decision
cards.use: need to show the steps of a process and where it branches
not: shows messages between systems in time order

cards.subject: A user flow
says: shows the path a person takes through a product to reach a goal
lays out screens and the choices that lead between them
cards.use: want to plan how a user gets from sign-up to first success
not: describes how servers communicate

cards.subject: A swimlane diagram
says: assigns each step to the person or team responsible using parallel lanes
exposes handoffs between teams
cards.use: need to show who is responsible for each step of a process
not: shows the states of a single object

cards.subject: An architecture diagram
says: shows the components of a system and the connections between them
helps newcomers see what talks to what
cards.use: want to explain the main parts of a system to a new developer
not: lists every field in a database table

cards.subject: A system context diagram
says: shows the system as one box surrounded by its users and external systems
leaves out the internal structure
cards.use: need to show the boundary of a system and what it interacts with
not: shows the classes inside one component

cards.subject: A sequence diagram
says: shows messages between participants in time order along vertical lifelines
makes the order of calls in an interaction clear
cards.use: need to show who calls whom and in what order
not: shows the shape of the stored data

cards.subject: An entity-relationship diagram
says: shows data entities and the relationships between them
indicates how many of one entity can relate to another
cards.use: need to design or explain a database structure
not: shows the order of API calls over time

cards.subject: A state diagram
says: shows the states an object can be in and the transitions between them
makes illegal transitions easy to spot
cards.use: need to specify how an order or account moves through its lifecycle
not: assigns steps to teams in lanes

cards.subject: The C4 model
says: describes software at four zoom levels: context, containers, components and code
lets each audience pick the level of detail they need
cards.use: want diagrams at several levels of zoom for different readers
not: is a notation for drawing database tables

cards.subject: Diagram as code
says: describes a diagram in text that a tool renders
lets a diagram be versioned and diffed like source code
cards.use: want diagram changes to be reviewed in a pull request
not: makes the diagram impossible to edit without special software

cards.subject: A whiteboard
says: offers an unbounded shared canvas for informal sketching
is for exploring rather than for the final record
cards.use: want a place to sketch ideas with others
not: is the best long-term home for decisions

cards.subject: Dot voting
says: gives each participant a few votes to place on options
surfaces group preference quickly
cards.use: need to narrow many ideas down in a workshop
not: gives the facilitator the deciding vote

cards.subject: A facilitator
says: keeps a session on topic and balanced between voices
does not need to be the most senior person
cards.use: find that a workshop is dominated by one or two voices
not: decides the outcome of the workshop alone

cards.subject: Silent brainstorming
says: has people write ideas alone before discussing them
reduces anchoring on the first idea spoken aloud
cards.use: want ideas from quieter people before the discussion starts
not: lets the loudest person speak first to set direction

cards.subject: A retrospective board
says: collects what went well, what did not and what to change
ends with agreed actions for the next iteration
cards.use: want a team to reflect on how it worked together
not: plans the content of the next release

cards.subject: Capturing board outcomes
says: moves decisions and actions from the board into a lasting document
prevents conclusions disappearing when the board is cleared
cards.use: finish a workshop and want the results to last
not: means exporting a screenshot and deleting everything else

cards.subject: A frame
says: is a container that represents a screen or section and holds other layers
can clip content that extends beyond its edge
cards.use: want a container for a screen or a section of one
not: is a single image that cannot contain other layers

cards.subject: A vector graphic
says: is described by paths and shapes so it scales without losing sharpness
suits logos and icons
cards.use: need an icon that stays crisp at any size
not: is made of a fixed grid of pixels

cards.subject: A raster image
says: is made of pixels and loses sharpness when enlarged
suits photographs
cards.use: need to include a photograph in a design
not: scales to any size without losing sharpness

cards.subject: A component
says: is a reusable element whose instances stay linked to the main definition
updates every instance when the main definition changes
cards.use: keep recreating the same button in many places
not: copies the element so each copy is independent

cards.subject: A design system
says: combines reusable components, tokens and usage guidance
keeps products visually consistent across teams
cards.use: want many designers and developers to build consistent interfaces
not: is a single style sheet for one page

cards.subject: A variant
says: is one version of a component, such as a state or size, grouped under that component
lets one component cover hover, disabled and other states
cards.use: need a button in several sizes and states under one component
not: is an unrelated copy of a component

cards.subject: A design token
says: stores a design decision such as a colour or spacing value under a name
lets one change flow through every place the value is used
cards.use: want to change a brand colour everywhere in one edit
not: is a security credential for the design tool

cards.subject: Auto layout
says: makes a frame resize and reflow around its content
spaces its children by rules instead of by hand
cards.use: want a button to grow when its label gets longer
not: pins a layer to an edge of a resizing parent only

cards.subject: Constraints
says: control how a layer behaves when its parent frame is resized
pin a layer to an edge or let it scale with the parent
cards.use: want an element to stay anchored to the right as a frame widens
not: reflow all children according to padding and gap rules

cards.subject: A sketch
says: tests whether a basic idea or flow makes sense
costs only minutes to make and throw away
cards.use: want to test an idea as cheaply as possible
not: needs polished visuals to be useful

cards.subject: A wireframe
says: shows layout and structure without final colour or imagery
keeps attention on arrangement rather than appearance
cards.use: want feedback on the structure of a screen, not its looks
not: shows the final visual styling of the product

cards.subject: A mockup
says: shows the visual design of a screen without being interactive
lets stakeholders judge appearance
cards.use: want to show how the finished screen will look
not: links screens so people can tap through them

cards.subject: A clickable prototype
says: links screens so a user can tap through a flow
lets people attempt a task before anything is built
cards.use: need to see whether people can finish a task
not: contains the real back-end logic of the product

cards.subject: Fidelity
says: describes how closely a prototype resembles the final product
should be chosen to match the question being asked
cards.use: need to decide how detailed a prototype should be
not: is always better when it is higher

cards.subject: A coded prototype
says: tests behaviour a mock cannot show, such as speed or real data
costs more to build than a clickable mock
cards.use: need to test how something performs with real data
not: is the cheapest way to test whether a flow makes sense

cards.subject: Prototype labelling
says: tells viewers what is not real
stops a mock being mistaken for the finished product
cards.use: are about to show a polished prototype to stakeholders
not: is only necessary for rough sketches

cards.subject: A Wizard of Oz test
says: has a person secretly perform the work the product will later automate
tests demand for a feature before building it
cards.use: want to test an automated feature without building the automation
not: is a test of the product's load capacity

cards.subject: Design handoff
says: passes finished design intent from designers to developers
works best as an ongoing conversation rather than a single event
cards.use: finish a design and need developers to build it
not: ends the designer's involvement

cards.subject: Inspect mode
says: lets a developer read measurements, colours and fonts from a design file
reduces guesswork when building from a mockup
cards.use: need exact spacing and colour values from a design
not: edits the design file for the developer

cards.subject: A design link on the ticket
says: connects a design file to the ticket it supports
keeps the reason for a design findable from the work item
cards.use: want developers to find the right design from an issue
not: replaces the need to describe acceptance criteria

cards.subject: An edge-state spec
says: specifies empty, loading, error and long-text cases beyond the happy path
prevents developers from inventing those states themselves
cards.use: find that a design shows only the ideal case
not: is only relevant to backend work

cards.subject: A responsive spec
says: describes how a layout changes across screen sizes
names the breakpoints where the layout changes
cards.use: need to tell developers how a design adapts to small screens
not: shows only one desktop layout

cards.subject: An early developer review
says: catches interactions that are hard to build before the design is polished
keeps the build estimate realistic
cards.use: want to find feasibility problems before design work is finished
not: happens only after the feature is shipped

cards.subject: A shared token file
says: keeps named design values shared between the design file and the codebase
lets a colour change in one source reach both design and code
cards.use: find that colours differ between the design file and the live site
not: is exported once and never kept in sync

cards.subject: A component mapping
says: pairs each design component with its code counterpart
stops designers and developers building duplicate versions
cards.use: want designers and developers to share one set of building blocks
not: lists only the colours used in the product
like: A design link on the ticket

cards.subject: A slide deck
says: presents a plan as a sequence of slides to an audience
supports a spoken explanation rather than replacing it
cards.use: need to walk an audience through a plan
not: is the best format for a long reference manual

cards.subject: The one-message rule
says: limits each slide to a single takeaway
keeps slides readable at a glance
cards.use: find that slides are crowded with several points
not: says a slide must contain at least five bullet points

cards.subject: An opening ask
says: states what you need from the audience before the supporting detail
lets listeners judge the detail against a clear decision
cards.use: want a decision from the audience at the end of a meeting
not: is saved for the final slide as a surprise

cards.subject: A shared link
says: shows every viewer the latest version of a deck
can expose unreleased work if anyone with the link may open it
cards.use: want an audience to always see the current version
not: freezes a snapshot that never changes

cards.subject: A PDF export
says: preserves a deck's appearance in a format almost any device can open
survives the original tool becoming unavailable
cards.use: need a portable copy of a deck that does not depend on the tool
not: keeps the deck editable in the original tool

cards.subject: Appendix slides
says: hold backup detail for questions without lengthening the main story
stay out of the main sequence of the talk
cards.use: want detail ready for questions but out of the presentation
not: are shown first so the audience sees all the data

cards.subject: Situation, complication, resolution
says: frames a story as context, then a problem, then the proposed answer
makes a recommendation feel like the natural next step
cards.use: need to structure a persuasive presentation
not: begins with the conclusion hidden until the end of the appendix

cards.subject: An issue
says: describes one unit of work, bug or request with an owner and a status
is the basic record of an issue tracker
cards.use: want one trackable record for a piece of work
not: is a conversation in a chat channel

cards.subject: A Kanban board
says: shows work as cards moving through columns
makes the current state of work visible at a glance
cards.use: want to see where every item of work stands
not: fixes a set of work for a timebox

cards.subject: A workflow status
says: marks where an issue is in its lifecycle, such as open or done
maps to the columns of a board
cards.use: want to know how far along an issue is
not: tags an issue with a category such as bug or design

cards.subject: An epic
says: groups related issues under a larger goal
is delivered by finishing the issues inside it
cards.use: need to track a large goal made of many issues
not: is a single small task

cards.subject: A sprint
says: is a fixed-length timebox in which a team commits to a set of work
ends with a review of what was delivered
cards.use: want to work in short, repeated cycles of fixed length
not: lets work flow continuously with no set period

cards.subject: Acceptance criteria
says: state the conditions that make an issue done
give the tester and developer the same target
cards.use: want a clear test of whether an issue is finished
not: describe how long the work will take

cards.subject: A good bug report
says: gives steps to reproduce, expected result and actual result
lets another person see the problem without asking questions
cards.use: need to report a defect so that someone else can fix it
not: says only that something is broken

cards.subject: A WIP limit
says: caps how many items may sit in a column at once
exposes bottlenecks by stopping new work starting
cards.use: find that too many items are started and few are finished
not: sets a deadline for each item

cards.subject: Issue triage
says: reviews new issues to decide priority, owner or closure
keeps the backlog from filling with unreviewed items
cards.use: find that new issues pile up without a decision
not: fixes each issue in order of arrival

cards.subject: Version history
says: lets you view and restore earlier states of a document
shows who changed what and when
cards.use: need to recover an earlier state of a document
not: prevents anyone from editing the document

cards.subject: A comment thread
says: attaches a discussion to a specific part of a document
can be resolved once the point is settled
cards.use: want to discuss one specific paragraph without editing it
not: changes the text of the document

cards.subject: Suggestion mode
says: records proposed edits for the owner to accept or reject
leaves the original text visible until a decision is made
cards.use: want to propose changes without overwriting the author's text
not: commits edits immediately for all readers

cards.subject: Real-time co-editing
says: shows several people's changes in one document at once
merges simultaneous edits automatically
cards.use: need several people to write in one document together
not: requires each person to work on a separate copy

cards.subject: Permission levels
says: separate who may view, comment and edit
let an owner give each person only the access they need
cards.use: want a client to read a document but not change it
not: give everyone the same access by default

cards.subject: A single source of truth
says: avoids divergent copies by keeping one live document that everyone links to
means people share a link rather than an attached copy
cards.use: find that several versions of a plan are circulating
not: is achieved by emailing the latest attachment to everyone

cards.subject: A named version
says: marks a meaningful milestone in a document's history
is easier to return to than an unlabelled automatic save
cards.use: want to mark the version that was approved
not: stops later edits being made

cards.subject: Link sharing scope
says: decides whether only named people or anyone with the link can open a document
should be checked before sending a link outside the team
cards.use: are about to send a link to unreleased work
not: only affects how the link looks

cards.subject: An audit log
says: records who changed or shared what and when
helps investigate unexpected access or edits
cards.use: need to find out who shared a document externally
not: restores deleted content automatically

cards.subject: A naming convention
says: makes names predictable so files can be found without opening them
is agreed once and then followed by the team
cards.use: want files to be findable by name
not: is chosen by each person individually

cards.subject: A date prefix in YYYY-MM-DD form
says: puts the year first so alphabetical order is chronological
avoids ambiguity between day-first and month-first dates
cards.use: want files to sort in date order by name
not: makes files sort by author name

cards.subject: A final in a file name
says: invites a later 'final-final' file because the word describes a moment rather than a version
is a poor substitute for version history
cards.use: see a file named final_v3_really_final
not: guarantees that nobody will edit the file again

cards.subject: A shallow folder hierarchy
says: keeps files within a few clicks
makes it easier to know where a file belongs
cards.use: find that people cannot locate files in deep folders
not: improves with ever more nested subfolders

cards.subject: One home per document
says: prevents duplicate copies drifting apart
lets other places link to it instead of copying it
cards.use: find the same document saved in several places
not: means copies are kept in every team folder for safety

cards.subject: Structuring by access
says: groups content by who may see it
allows permissions to be set once at folder level
cards.use: need to keep client work separate from internal drafts
not: ignores who needs to see the content

cards.subject: Alt text
says: describes the purpose of an image to people who cannot see it
is read aloud by screen readers
cards.use: want an informative image to make sense to a screen reader user
not: is a caption displayed under the image for all readers

cards.subject: A contrast checker
says: calculates the contrast ratio between text and background colours
compares the result against accessibility thresholds
cards.use: need to check whether text is readable against its background
not: checks whether a page works with the keyboard

cards.subject: WCAG
says: is the W3C's set of guidelines for accessible web content
organises requirements under perceivable, operable, understandable and robust
defines conformance levels A, AA and AAA
cards.use: need a recognised standard to measure accessibility against
not: is a software tool that fixes accessibility problems automatically

cards.subject: An automated accessibility scanner
says: finds problems that rules can detect, such as missing alt text or low contrast
cannot judge whether alt text is meaningful
cards.use: want a fast first pass over many pages
not: finds every accessibility problem on a page

cards.subject: A screen reader
says: reads on-screen content aloud or sends it to a braille display
depends on correct semantic structure to be usable
cards.use: need to understand how blind users experience a page
not: magnifies the screen for people with low vision

cards.subject: Keyboard-only testing
says: checks that every function works without a mouse and that focus is visible
reveals broken tab order and keyboard traps
cards.use: need to confirm that a page can be used without a mouse
not: checks the contrast of text colours

cards.subject: A colour-blindness simulator
says: previews a design as people with colour vision deficiency see it
shows whether meaning is carried by colour alone
cards.use: want to see if a chart relies on red and green alone
not: measures contrast ratios

cards.subject: An ARIA label
says: supplies an accessible name when no visible text provides one
should not replace a native element that already does the job
cards.use: have an icon-only button with no visible text
not: makes a div behave like a button without further work

cards.subject: Manual accessibility testing
says: judges what automated tools cannot, such as reading order and clear link text
uses real assistive technology to check the experience
cards.use: need to verify the experience beyond what a scanner reports
not: is unnecessary once a scanner reports zero errors

cards.subject: The Moksy catalogue's families
says: groups apps into families such as roadmaps, documents and design
gives each family a unit that an integration carries
cards.use: need to see how Moksy organises its planning and design integrations
not: lists each app as an unrelated one-off build

cards.subject: The status works today
says: means a path Moksy already ships carries the app with only a URL, file, link or MCP entry needed from the app
needs no work on the app side beyond providing one of those
cards.use: need to know which apps are usable now with nothing extra
not: requires a native adapter to be built first

cards.subject: The status through a hub
says: means the app works now using an automation hub's generic webhook and HTTP steps plus a Moksy API key
relies on a hub rather than a native connector
cards.use: need to know which apps connect through an automation platform
not: means the app is retired

cards.subject: The status with a script
says: means only Moksy's public API called from the app's own scripting carries the connection
has no built-in connector or hub recipe
cards.use: need to know which apps reach Moksy only by custom scripting
not: means a hub template is available

cards.subject: The status adapter planned
says: means only a first-class connector would carry the app and that connector is not built
is not yet usable
cards.use: need to know which apps wait on a native connector
not: means the app already works through a hub

cards.subject: The status not yet
says: means the app offers nothing Moksy can use
has no path available
cards.use: need to know which apps cannot be integrated at all
not: means a connector is planned

cards.subject: Effort grade E0
says: means there is nothing to do to connect the app
goes with apps that already work today
cards.use: need to know which integrations need no work
not: means a native adapter must be built

cards.subject: Effort grade E1
says: means a hub template or worked example is needed
falls between nothing to do and a native adapter
cards.use: need to know which integrations need a template or example
not: means nothing at all needs doing

cards.subject: Effort grade E2
says: means a native adapter must be built
is the highest effort grade
cards.use: need to know which integrations require a first-class connector
not: means a hub template is enough

cards.subject: A roadmap item in Moksy
says: can start a Briefing
is the unit that moves in the product management and roadmaps family
cards.use: want a roadmap item to begin a Moksy workflow
not: becomes an invoice

cards.subject: Interview notes and feedback in Moksy
says: are the Sources a problem statement is built from
are the unit that moves in the user research and feedback family
cards.use: want evidence to feed a Moksy problem statement
not: are deployment logs

cards.subject: A design file in Moksy
says: is cited in the Blueprint
is the unit that moves in the design and prototyping family
sits next to the requirements it supports
cards.use: want designs linked to Moksy requirements
not: replaces the requirements document
like: A design link on the ticket

cards.subject: A whiteboard in Moksy
says: is catalogued as an input to a Briefing
can be attached to a Blueprint
cards.use: want a board to feed a Moksy Briefing
not: is reached through a native adapter only

cards.subject: A Blueprint as a deck
says: is the intended pattern in the presentations and publishing family
can be presented as a slide deck or published as a page
cards.use: want to present a Blueprint to stakeholders
not: must be exported from a spreadsheet first

cards.subject: The generated catalogue file
says: is produced from source files
must not be edited by hand
cards.use: want to change an entry in the Moksy catalogue document
not: is the place where entries should be edited directly

cards.subject: The ggsocial DEPLOY.md
says: records traps learned the hard way
notes that a deploy sync with delete can wipe the production secrets file
notes that the server's login shell cannot parse some commands
cards.use: want an example of operational knowledge kept in a repository
not: is a wiki page maintained outside the repository

cards.subject: The gglearn docs folder and README
says: keep documentation in the repository alongside the code
are reviewed with the code
cards.use: want to know where gglearn's documentation lives
not: live only in a wiki

qa.q: What is the main job of a product roadmap?
qa.right: To communicate the direction and priorities of a product over time
wrong: To list every bug found in testing
To store the final source code
qa.why: A roadmap shows where the product is heading and why.

qa.q: What does a user interview mainly give you?
qa.right: Rich qualitative detail about why people behave as they do
wrong: A statistically exact count of users
qa.why: Interviews explain behaviour but involve few people.

qa.q: Why use a README?
qa.right: So a newcomer can learn what a project is and how to start without asking anyone
wrong: To record every past decision in full
qa.why: A README is the front door of a repository.

qa.q: Which diagram uses a diamond for a yes-or-no decision?
qa.right: A flowchart
qa.why: Flowcharts use diamonds for decision points.

qa.q: What does alt text do?
qa.right: Describes the purpose of an image to people who cannot see it
qa.why: Screen readers read alt text aloud.

qa.q: What is the difference between a vector and a raster image?
qa.right: A vector image is made of paths and scales cleanly, a raster image is made of pixels
wrong: A raster image scales cleanly, a vector image is made of pixels
They are the same file type
A vector image can only be a photograph
qa.why: Vectors suit icons and logos; rasters suit photos.

qa.q: Which tool helps you choose the minimum set of requirements for a release by labelling items must, should, could and won't?
qa.right: MoSCoW prioritisation
qa.why: MoSCoW buckets requirements.

qa.q: A team wants quantitative evidence of which of two page designs performs better. What should they run?
qa.right: An A/B test
qa.why: An A/B test compares variants with separate user groups.

qa.q: Why is a page owner useful in a wiki?
qa.right: One named person is responsible for the page staying correct
wrong: Only that person may read it
It stops the page being searched
It makes the page load faster
qa.why: Ownership fights stale pages.

qa.q: What does a swimlane diagram add that a plain flowchart lacks?
qa.right: Lanes that show who is responsible for each step
qa.why: Lanes expose handoffs between teams.

qa.q: What is the benefit of a component in a design tool?
qa.right: Instances stay linked, so changing the main component updates all of them
wrong: Each copy is independent of the others
It exports the file to code automatically
It removes the need for a grid
qa.why: Components keep reusable elements consistent.

qa.q: What do acceptance criteria state?
qa.right: The conditions that make an issue done
wrong: How long the issue will take
Which sprint the issue was created in
qa.why: They give tester and developer the same target.

qa.q: Which question does an automated accessibility scanner fail to answer?
qa.right: Whether the alt text actually describes the image meaningfully
wrong: Whether a colour contrast is too low
Whether a form field lacks a label
qa.why: Rules detect presence, not meaning.

qa.q: Which file name sorts in chronological order alphabetically?
qa.right: 2026-03-14-planning-notes
qa.why: Year-first ISO dates sort chronologically.

qa.q: Which prioritisation method divides estimated benefit by effort and discounts guesses with a confidence factor?
qa.right: RICE scoring
qa.why: RICE uses reach, impact, confidence and effort.

qa.q: What is the difference between a card sort and a tree test?
qa.right: A card sort asks people to build groupings, a tree test checks whether they can find items in a given structure
wrong: A tree test asks people to build groupings, a card sort checks findability
They are two names for the same method
A card sort needs working software, a tree test does not
qa.why: Card sorts generate structure; tree tests validate it.

qa.q: A UI design shows one wide screen with no empty, loading or error states. What is missing?
qa.right: An edge-state specification
qa.why: Developers otherwise invent the missing states.

qa.q: What does a WIP limit expose?
qa.right: Bottlenecks, by stopping new work starting while a column is full
qa.why: Limits force the team to finish before starting.

qa.q: What is the effect of having a design token for a brand colour?
qa.right: Changing the token updates every place the colour is used
wrong: The colour can no longer be changed
The colour is hidden from developers
Each use must be edited separately
qa.why: Tokens give a value one name.

qa.q: Which description fits Auto layout rather than Constraints?
qa.right: A frame that resizes and reflows around its content
wrong: A layer pinned to the right edge of a parent
qa.why: Constraints pin to parents; auto layout reflows children.

qa.q: What is the purpose of silent brainstorming?
qa.right: To reduce anchoring on the first idea spoken aloud
wrong: To save time by skipping discussion entirely
To let the senior person choose
To produce a single idea quickly
qa.why: People write alone first, then discuss.

qa.q: Which sentence best describes docs as code?
qa.right: Documentation lives in version control and is reviewed with the code
wrong: Documentation is generated only from comments
Documentation is stored in the wiki and copied to the repo yearly
qa.why: One pull request can change both.

qa.q: What does a sequence diagram show best?
qa.right: Messages between participants in time order
wrong: The shape of the stored data
The users of a system as one box
The pixel layout of a screen
qa.why: Vertical lifelines show order of calls.

qa.q: In Moksy's catalogue, what does the status 'works today' mean?
qa.right: A path Moksy already ships carries the app, with only a URL, file, link or MCP entry needed
wrong: The app needs a native connector that is not built
The app works only through an automation hub
Only Moksy's API called from the app's own scripting carries it
qa.why: It needs nothing from the app side beyond one of those.

qa.q: Which Moksy catalogue effort grade means a native adapter must be built?
qa.right: E2
wrong: No grade; native adapters are never needed
qa.why: E0 is nothing to do, E1 is a hub template or worked example, E2 is a native adapter.

qa.q: What does the Kano model predict about delighters?
qa.right: They tend to become basic expectations over time
wrong: They are the same as bugs
They are always the cheapest features to build
qa.why: Today's surprise becomes tomorrow's baseline.

qa.q: Which method best uncovers workarounds people forget to mention in interviews?
qa.right: Contextual inquiry
qa.why: Observing real work reveals workarounds.

qa.q: What is the purpose of the C4 model's levels?
qa.right: Letting each audience pick a zoom level from context to code
qa.why: Context, containers, components and code.

qa.q: Why is diagram as code useful?
qa.right: Diagram changes can be versioned and diffed like source code
wrong: It makes diagrams impossible to render
It removes the need for review
qa.why: Text sources go through pull requests.

qa.q: When is an ARIA label appropriate?
qa.right: For an icon-only button that has no visible text to name it
wrong: On a native button that already has a text label, to override it
To make a div behave fully like a button without keyboard support
To hide text from sighted users
qa.why: ARIA supplies a name only where none exists and should not replace native elements.

qa.q: Which testing step is needed even when a scanner reports zero errors?
qa.right: Manual testing with assistive technology and keyboard
qa.why: Scanners cannot judge reading order or clear link text.

qa.q: What does a Wizard of Oz test tell you?
qa.right: Whether people want an automated feature, before anyone builds the automation
wrong: How fast the server responds under load
Whether the colours meet contrast thresholds
qa.why: A person secretly does the work behind the interface.

qa.q: Why must the Moksy catalogue markdown file not be edited by hand?
qa.right: It is generated from source files, so manual edits would be overwritten and drift from the truth
wrong: Only hub vendors may change it
qa.why: Edit the sources and regenerate.

qa.q: A team's wiki page says deployments use script A, but the repo now uses script B. What should you do first?
qa.right: Move the authoritative steps into the repo next to the script and leave a pointer in the wiki
wrong: Add a bold warning at the top of the wiki page
Ask the team to remember the change
Delete the wiki page without a replacement
qa.why: Code-coupled docs belong with the code.

qa.q: A stakeholder sees a polished clickable prototype and asks why the feature is not live. What would have prevented this?
qa.right: Labelling it as a prototype and stating what is not real
wrong: Making it look rougher without explanation
Removing the stakeholder from the review
qa.why: Fidelity should match the question and be labelled.

qa.q: You have run five interviews and a heavyweight platform is proposed. What is a sensible first step?
qa.right: Start with a shared document and a sheet, and set a trigger for moving to a platform
wrong: Stop researching until a platform is chosen
Store the notes in individual inboxes
qa.why: Low volume rarely justifies heavy tooling; check export, API, permissions and deletion first.

qa.q: You are about to send a deck link to a client and the deck contains unreleased pricing work. What should you check?
qa.right: Who can open the link, whether it is limited to named people
wrong: The font size of the notes
Whether the deck has a dark theme
qa.why: Open links can expose unreleased work.

qa.q: Customers keep asking for an 'export to spreadsheet' button. What is the best next step?
qa.right: Ask what they are trying to achieve before deciding on the feature
wrong: Add it to the roadmap with a date
qa.why: The request may hide a different underlying need.

qa.q: A button label in your design grows longer in translation and overflows. Which feature solves this best?
qa.right: Auto layout so the frame grows with the content
wrong: Rasterising the button as an image
qa.why: Auto layout reflows around content.

qa.q: Your team's backlog has hundreds of unreviewed items. What practice helps?
qa.right: Regular triage to set priority, owner or closure
qa.why: Triage keeps the backlog meaningful.

qa.q: A research recording contains a participant's name and opinions about colleagues. Another team asks for it. What should you do?
qa.right: Check consent and share an anonymised summary instead of the raw recording
wrong: Post it in a public channel
qa.why: Raw material needs consent and access control.

qa.q: A chart uses only red and green to show good and bad. What is the problem and the fix?
qa.right: Colour alone carries the meaning, so add labels or patterns
wrong: The chart is too small, so enlarge it
There are too many colours, so add more
Nothing; red and green are universal
qa.why: Colour-blind users cannot distinguish them.

qa.q: A scanner shows zero accessibility errors but users report they cannot complete checkout by keyboard. How do you reconcile this?
qa.right: Scanners miss problems like tab order and keyboard traps, so test manually
wrong: The scanner is broken and should be replaced
qa.why: Automated tools only catch a portion of issues.

qa.q: Two designers keep building their own versions of a card component. What practice fixes this?
qa.right: Maintain one shared component library with a code mapping
wrong: Ask them to use different colours
Export the cards as PNG files
qa.why: One source of building blocks avoids duplicates.

qa.q: A decision made six months ago is being reargued because nobody remembers why. What was missing?
qa.right: A decision log or decision record with context and options
qa.why: Recording the why saves reopening settled questions.

qa.q: A designer hands off a file with only the main flow designed. What is likely to happen in build?
qa.right: Developers invent empty, loading and error states without design input
qa.why: Edge states need to be specified.

qa.q: A roadmap with exact dates for all next-year items keeps slipping and eroding trust. What would you change?
qa.right: Move to a now-next-later or outcome-based format that avoids dates for distant items
qa.why: Distant certainty is false precision.

qa.q: You need to design navigation for a new site and have no structure yet. Which method first, and which second?
qa.right: A card sort first to generate groupings, then a tree test to check findability
wrong: A tree test first, then a card sort
An A/B test first, then a diary study
qa.why: Generate structure, then validate it.

qa.q: In the Moksy catalogue an app has status 'adapter planned'. What can you say about it today?
qa.right: It cannot be connected until a native connector is built
wrong: It works now through any hub
It is already usable with a URL
qa.why: Only a first-class connector would carry it, and that is not built.

qa.q: A designer exports every icon as a PNG at one size and developers complain icons look blurry on large screens. What would you change?
qa.right: Export icons as vector files so they scale cleanly
wrong: Convert the icons to a photograph
qa.why: Vectors scale without losing sharpness.

qa.q: A workshop board has 40 sticky notes and the team votes with three dots each. One person votes for all three on their own idea. What does the facilitator do?
qa.right: Agree up front that each person places each dot on a different option, and note the result as input rather than a decision
wrong: Let the vote stand and ship it
qa.why: Dot voting is a signal, and rules should be agreed first.

qa.q: Your team cites 'a design file shows what but not why'. How do you keep the why?
qa.right: Link the design from the requirement and write the decision it supported
qa.why: Traceability preserves the reason for design choices.

qa.q: A support team's tickets suggest that a feature is hated, but your voting board shows no complaints. What explains the gap?
qa.right: Tickets over-represent people who hit trouble while the voting board hears from those motivated to vote
qa.why: Each channel has its own bias, so triangulate.

qa.q: An engineer asks whether the ggsocial DEPLOY.md should move to the wiki. Which answer matches the stated practice?
qa.right: Keep it in the repository, because code-coupled operational knowledge is easily lost in a wiki
wrong: Move it so that non-developers can edit it
Store it on the production server only
qa.why: The DEPLOY.md records traps learned the hard way alongside the code.

qa.q: A team uses a stakeholder-friendly roadmap but a leader asks, 'Which interviews justify this item?' and nobody knows. What is the root cause and fix?
qa.right: Evidence is not linked to decisions, so link roadmap items back to the research that justifies them
wrong: The roadmap has too few columns
qa.why: A roadmap should point back to evidence.

qa.q: A team shares one deck as an email attachment and finds three versions in circulation. What change fixes it?
qa.right: Share a link to a single live deck and keep a PDF export for portability
wrong: Attach the file again with 'final' in the name
qa.why: A link shows the latest version; the export is a backup.

qa.q: Which of these is a good bug report?
qa.right: Steps to reproduce, what you expected and what actually happened
qa.why: A good report lets someone else see the problem.

qa.q: What is the purpose of dot voting?
qa.right: To narrow many ideas down quickly by giving each person a few votes
wrong: To give the facilitator the final decision
qa.why: It surfaces group preference.

qa.q: Where do decisions and actions belong after a whiteboard workshop?
qa.right: In a lasting document, not just on the board
wrong: In the chat channel topic only
qa.why: Boards are cleared; documents last.

qa.q: A new teammate cannot find a file named 'Final_v2_NEW.docx'. What naming change helps most?
qa.right: Use a descriptive title with a date prefix and rely on version history
wrong: Store it in a deeper folder
qa.why: Names should be predictable and versions tracked by the tool.
